newsitem.title: UK: Britain hopes for N.Irish settlement by May.
newsitem.headline: Britain hopes for N.Irish settlement by May.

text.p: Britain tried on Wednesday to inject urgency into Northern Ireland's peace talks by warning it would hold only one more meeting with Sinn Fein, the political wing of the IRA, unless the guerrillas announced a ceasefire.

Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam told parliament the talks risked running into the sand unless progress was made soon and she sought to concentrate minds by fixing May 1998 as a target date for a lasting political settlement.

"This is the time when we hope a settlement and final vote and referendum could be held," she said. Sinn Fein is banned from multi-party talks on the future of the British-ruled province until the Irish Republican Army announces a truce.
Mowlam said she hoped to settle the controversial issue of scrapping arms held by rival guerrilla groups by the end of the month with an eye to launching substantive talks in the autumn.
"I think the talks are in danger of running into the sands and I think progress must be made as soon as possible," she said.

"We are working closely with the Irish government and with the parties to try to see if we can get the question of decommissioning illegal weapons settled in the next couple of weeks which would allow us to move on to substantive negotiations in September," she added.

New Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair has authorised two rounds of explanatory talks between government officials and Sinn Fein since he took office on May 1 and Mowlam said a request had been received on Tuesday for a third meeting.
She said she was willing to comply but it would be the last meeting unless the IRA unequivocally restored, in word and in deed, the ceasefire it broke in February 1996.
The IRA is fighting to end British rule and unite the province with the overwhelmingly Catholic Irish Republic.
"We will not go on indefinitely. We've no intention of doing that at all... Another meeting is likely but that will be it," she said.

Mowlam stressed that the talks so far had been designed to clarify points for Sinn Fein. She said there was no question of admitting it to the multi-party talks that resumed in Belfast on June 3 without a ceasefire.

"It is not up to us any more. We have made our position clear. The ball is in the court of Sinn Fein. If progress is to be made to make the talks inclusive, then it is up to them to make the move," she added.
